# DAC2B: other official flows by recipient

## What it is

DAC2B reports other official flows (OOF) and officially supported export credits from each donor to each recipient country, region, and income group. Donors include DAC countries, non-DAC reporters, and multilateral lenders reporting their own non-concessional lending. Its measures are:

- OOF grants, loan disbursements, loan repayments, equity, interest received, offsetting entries for debt relief on OOF claims, and gross and net OOF
- Export credits gross, repayments and net, and offsetting entries for debt relief on export credit claims
- Official non-concessional flows, net, which combine OOF and export credits, and from 2023, private sector instruments
- Private sector instruments, net

Values are in USD at current and constant prices.

## Reporting level

DAC2B publishes bilateral DAC donors' figures only against regional and income-group aggregates, such as sub-Saharan Africa, LDCs or ACP states, and country-level detail comes from multilateral lenders such as IBRD. A bilateral donor with no figure for a country has its flows to that country inside those aggregates.

The DAC countries total carries country-level OOF that no published individual donor accounts for, so a country total built by summing individual donors differs from the aggregate.

## Agreement with the CRS

The OECD compiles DAC2B from donors' CRS reporting, so the two agree for multilateral lenders and for donor totals across all developing countries. Beyond the country detail that DAC2B holds back for bilateral donors, which the CRS shows, they disagree in three places. Some donors' OOF appears in DAC2B with no matching CRS records, Japan's being the largest case. DAC2B's gross OOF is net of amounts received back on grants and leaves out guarantees, both of which CRS OOF records include. Export credits appear in DAC2B but not as CRS records.

## Double counting and aggregates

Donors and recipients are both provided as individual entries and as aggregates, and a sum that includes an aggregate alongside its members double counts.

- Donor aggregates are official donors (DAC countries, non-DAC countries, and multilaterals), DAC countries, DAC countries plus EU Institutions, DAC EU countries, DAC EU countries plus EU Institutions, the G7, non-DAC countries, other countries, and multilaterals. Multilaterals also split into sub-aggregates (the UN, the World Bank, the World Bank Group, regional development banks, and others) that overlap one another and the multilaterals total.
- Recipient aggregates are regions, income groups, other country groups, the developing countries total, multilateral recipients, and all recipients. Regions overlap (Africa contains Northern Africa and Sub-Saharan Africa, and Sub-Saharan Africa overlaps Eastern, Middle, Southern, and Western Africa), and most regions have an "unspecified" bucket for amounts not allocated to a country. Income groups come in DAC and World Bank classifications. Other country groups (LDCs, SIDS, LLDCs, HIPCs, ACP states, fragile contexts, and basin groupings) cut across regions and income groups.

A regional total built from individual countries misses the region's unspecified bucket.

The measures include gross and net totals alongside their components. Net OOF is gross OOF minus repayments, and official non-concessional flows combine OOF, export credits and, from 2023, private sector instruments. Adding measures across levels counts flows twice.

Total official flows to a recipient equals its ODA plus OOF. Export credits include privately extended credits and are excluded from the total.

## Particularities

Net flows to a recipient are negative in years when repayments exceed new lending.

Export credits are counted at face value.

# DAC2A: ODA disbursements to countries and regions

## What it is

DAC2A reports ODA disbursements from each donor to each recipient country, region, and income group. It holds gross ODA, net ODA, and their components (grants, loans, debt relief, technical co-operation, humanitarian aid, and others). All values are disbursements in USD at current and constant prices.

Donors include DAC countries, non-DAC reporters, multilateral agencies reporting their own outflows (such as IDA, the regional development banks, UN agencies, Gavi, and the Global Fund), and private foundations.

The table also carries recipient-side indicators, ODA per capita, and ODA as a percentage of the recipient's GNI.

## Totals against DAC1

At the developing countries total, a donor's DAC2A net ODA equals its DAC1 bilateral ODA in net disbursements. In-donor refugee costs, administrative costs, and similar items sit in "developing countries, unspecified", so the sum of individual countries is lower than DAC1 bilateral ODA, and much lower for donors with high refugee costs.

DAC2A is provided on a cash basis. Its net ODA subtracts loan repayments, so it will not match the grant-equivalent headline in DAC1 for years from 2018.

## Imputed multilateral ODA

Imputed multilateral ODA is the OECD's estimate of how much of each donor's core multilateral contributions reached each recipient. It is published for DAC countries, non-DAC countries, and EU Institutions. It takes each agency's geographical breakdown of its gross disbursements from core resources in the reference year and applies that breakdown to the donor's core contributions to the agency. It is a memo item, outside net ODA, and it does not sum to DAC1 multilateral ODA.

Bilateral net ODA plus imputed multilateral ODA gives a donor's total contribution to a recipient. When you read a figure on this convention, say in the reply that the bilateral part is net and why: "net bilateral, as DAC counts a donor's total contribution". The OECD figure attributes core contributions to recipients, while ONE's imputed multilateral sectors dataset attributes them to sectors with a different method, so the two do not reconcile.

## Double counting and aggregates

Donors and recipients are provided as both individual entries and aggregates, and a sum that includes an aggregate alongside its members double counts.

- Donor aggregates are official donors (DAC countries, non-DAC countries, and multilaterals), DAC countries, DAC countries plus EU Institutions, DAC EU countries, DAC EU countries plus EU Institutions, the G7, non-DAC countries, other countries, multilaterals, and private donors. Multilaterals also split into sub-aggregates (the UN, the World Bank, the World Bank Group, regional development banks, and others) that overlap one another and the multilaterals total.
- Recipient aggregates are regions, income groups, other country groups, the developing countries total, and all recipients. Regions overlap (Africa contains Northern Africa and Sub-Saharan Africa, and Sub-Saharan Africa overlaps Eastern, Middle, Southern, and Western Africa), and most regions have an "unspecified" bucket for amounts not allocated to a country. Other country groups (SIDS, LLDCs, HIPCs, ACP states, fragile contexts, basin groupings, and more advanced developed countries) cut across regions and income groups. Income groups (LDCs, other low-income, lower-middle-income, and upper-middle-income countries, and unallocated by income) come in DAC and World Bank classifications. The developing countries total includes "developing countries, unspecified", and all recipients equals the developing countries total plus multilateral recipients.

Multilateral agencies appear as both recipients and donors. Multilateral recipients hold donors' core contributions to IDA, UNICEF, EU Institutions, and others. A total that counts money going into multilaterals and money they provide to developing countries counts it twice.

The two aggregates that add EU Institutions to member states (DAC countries plus EU Institutions, and DAC EU countries plus EU Institutions) contain both the members' contributions to EU Institutions and EU Institutions' own ODA. The members' contributions sit under multilateral recipients, so to the developing countries total these aggregates count EU money once. To all recipients they count it twice.

A recipient's total receipts are the sum of bilateral donors and multilateral donors. Adding a donor's imputed multilateral ODA to the multilateral agencies' own outflows counts the same money twice.

A regional total built from individual countries misses the region's unspecified bucket.

## Particularities

Net ODA can be negative for a donor-recipient pair when loan repayments or debt-relief offsets exceed new disbursements.

The DAC list of ODA recipients changes as countries graduate, and historical data include a separate group of countries in transition. A long series for one recipient can stop, and aggregate recipient totals shift as countries join or leave the list.

# Creditor Reporting System (CRS)

## What it is

The CRS is the OECD's activity-level database. Each record is a project, programme, or contribution reported by a provider. Reporters are DAC members, non-DAC countries that report to the DAC, multilateral organisations reporting their own outflows, and private foundations such as the Gates Foundation.

The main attributes are year, provider and agency, recipient country or region, purpose and sector, channel of delivery, aid type, finance type, flow category, commitment and disbursement amounts, grant equivalent, loan terms, policy markers, and text descriptions. Purposes roll up into sectors.

Amounts are provided in USD at current prices and at constant prices, deflated with the provider's own deflator. Multilaterals use the total DAC deflator. The constant-price base year moves with each release. Commitments and gross disbursements are reported at face value, and loan repayments are recorded separately. Grant equivalents exist for ODA flows and ODA-eligible private sector instruments from 2018.

## Coverage against DAC1

DAC1 is the authoritative total, and CRS totals will not match it exactly. The OECD measures CRS coverage against donors' DAC reporting, and some items are reported in aggregate in the CRS (administrative costs, scholarships, small technical co-operation). Historic gaps are larger.

- Commitments cover about 70% in 1995, over 90% in 2000, and nearly 100% from 2003.
- Disbursements cover less than 60% before 2002, around 90% from 2002, and nearly 100% from 2007. The OECD advises against using CRS disbursements for flows before 2002.
- Records start in 1973, and pre-1995 data are incomplete.
- Aid type was introduced for 2010 flows, and earlier years are partly back-mapped and incomplete.

## Distinctions that decide what a total means

The flow category separates the kinds of money: ODA, OOF other than export credits, officially supported export credits, private development finance from foundations, private sector instruments, private foreign direct investment, and other private flows at market terms. Private sector instruments are a separate category that an ODA total includes only by choice.

A bilateral/multilateral flag separates who controls the money.

- Bilateral flows
- Core contributions to multilateral organisations, recorded as inflows to the multilateral
- Core contributions to NGOs, other private bodies and public-private partnerships
- Multilateral outflows, reported by multilateral agencies only
- Private grants, reported by DAC members and private providers
- Ex-post reporting on NGO activities funded through core contributions
- Triangular co-operation

Aid type also flags core funding. Its core categories are support to NGOs and research institutes, contributions to multilateral institutions, and contributions to global funds, the last two split since 2022. Earmarked funding through multilaterals is bilateral. Its channel of delivery is a multilateral organisation, and it can carry any aid type, including projects, specific-purpose programmes, and pooled funds.

## Double counting and aggregates

Since the April 2026 release, the CRS includes providers' core contributions to multilaterals as records flagged as multilateral inflows. The OECD says these records must be excluded to calculate bilateral flows and avoid double counting.

The CRS in the DFO knowledge graph has these records filtered out, so it contains no providers' core contributions to multilaterals. CRS data drawn directly from the OECD most likely include them, and whether they are present is worth checking before any bilateral total is built.

A provider's core contribution to a multilateral and the multilateral's own outflows are the same money, just at two different points in time. A total across all reporters that keeps both counts it twice. Donor-side totals retain the contribution, and recipient-side and sector-wide totals retain the outflow.

Multilateral reporters include only core-funded activities in the CRS, so earmarked trust funds reported by a bilateral provider do not reappear as the multilateral's outflow. Foundation grants to Gavi or the Global Fund are private flows that then fund those organisations' outflows. A total that adds foundations and multilaterals counts that money twice.

Recipients include regional and unspecified buckets alongside countries, such as "developing countries, unspecified" and "South of Sahara, regional". A regional total from the CRS needs the countries plus the matching regional bucket. A country figure that includes a share of a regional or unspecified amount rests on an assumption about how that amount was spread.

## Particularities

Commitments are lumpy. A multi-year programme is committed in one year and disbursed over several, so commitment series jump and disbursement series lag.

The purpose list grows over time. COVID-19 control is one example. A subsector series can start mid-way through a time range. Broad sector totals include multisector and unallocated purposes, which are part of the total and belong to no single sector.

Policy markers (gender, climate, biodiversity, and others) are scored per activity. A significant-objective score counts the whole activity amount, and blank scores mean the activity was not screened. A share computed over all activities, screened and unscreened together, understates the marked share. The CRS in the DFO knowledge graph carries no policy markers, so a question that depends on them, such as climate- or gender-tagged ODA, cannot be answered from DFO data until policy markers are added, planned for autumn 2026.

Private sector instruments reported under the instrument approach, where each loan, equity stake, or guarantee to a company is recorded, appear in the CRS with a recipient and sector. Under the institutional approach, which records capital injections to development finance institutions, the money has no specific recipient country or sector.

CRS data are revised between annual releases. New reporters are added and records corrected, so results depend on the release.
